At approx. 00:47 to 00:49, Video 2 DOW-UAP-PR141 https://www.war.gov/UFO/release/06/#DOW-UAP-PR141-Unresolved-UAP-Report-Middle-East-2022,
as the feature moves from right to left, the slight changes in shape and their rate make me think of the flapping wings of a bird.

The AARO Video Description for DOW-UAP-PR141 refers to and describes a single UAP, but there are other apparently similar features at various times in the video,

The accompanying report https://www.war.gov/medialink/ufo/s...-UAP-D109_Mission-Report-Middle-East-2022.pdf refers to UAPs, plural.
I think this is a bit odd; presumably whoever wrote the video description at AARO noticed the other features? If they were considered not to be anomalous, it would be interesting to know why- again, they appear to be similar to the one feature whose movement is described.

The report says,

External Quote:

...THE UAPs WERE TRAVELLING AT VARIOUS SPEEDS BETWEEN 80-180 MPH. WE WERE UNABLE TO DETERMINE ALTITUDE. THE SIZE OF THE UAPs WERE APPROXIMATELY 1-2 METERS.

But if with an estimated size, known orientation relative to the camera, landscape features initially in view (and known location, altitude of the camera platform) shouldn't a range of possible altitudes have been calculable?
It is not clear how the approximate size was calculated.
Without an approximate altitude (and presumably distance), and a size estimate of uncertain origin, it's hard to see how speed could be reliably estimated.

Unless further information (perhaps an explanation for the size and speed estimates, values for altitude/ distance) emerge, the segment of footage 00:47 to 00:49, Video 2 DOW-UAP-PR141 makes me think the features are birds.

  • #17

So it seems more like a boilerplate report rather than even superficial technical details. Possibly even generated from checking some boxes in a form.

People should remember that drones like this have been in the air daily for years now. In many cases nothing of interest happens in the locations being surveilled. But reports must always be made after every flight, if even just to say "nothing happening". Because nothing happening is a valid and useful observation and provides information about the locations.

So when something is noticed, like these objects, it becomes something to report when otherwise there would be nothing interesting to report. But then you have to describe what you observed. When you don't have the ability to provide highly accurate measurements you have to estimate, based on your many hours experience looking at video like this. "Small" would not be acceptable, too vague, so you say "1-2 meters" which is about the smallest size range the system you are using will collect. Then they are moving, not super fast and not drifting like a balloon, so again you estimate, probably based on your knowledge of how fast the camera platform is moving, 'about the same as', 'faster than', 'much faster than'. And again you need to provide numbers, not just relative speeds. So 80-180, probably in the ball-park anyway.

People should remember these are reports of "business as usual" for the people who wrote them, these are not breathless reports of a once-in-a-lifetime event. You report what you can, and move on to the next days monitoring of video.

The same misspelling, "sporatically", might indicate the claimant copied details from another report, or one claimant uploaded similar reports for two different pieces of footage. Very curious.

Don't know what system this information was typed up on, but it probably did not have spell-check turned on. Reports like this contain too many abbreviations, acronyms and foreign names. Spell checkers would go nuts. So this in probably just a mistype at some point in the process that was just left as is.
